items.title: Half a Billion Christians Around the World Can’t Access the Bible, New Analysis Shows
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Concerning.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

While technology has greatly expanded the availability of Scripture, a perfect storm of calamities has kept the Bible out of the hands of half a billion Christians around the globe.

According to just-released data from the 2026 Bible Access List, the second such analysis from the Bible Access Initiative, 125 million believers are unable to access God’s Word in any format, even in countries where Scripture is technically allowed and safe to possess.

The report evaluates 106 countries and pinpoints where Christians face the greatest obstacles to accessing the Bible, some entirely and others in part.

“We often hear that the Bible is more accessible than ever, but we must not confuse availability with access,” Wybo Nicolai, co-founder of the Bible Access List, said in a statement about the latest data. “Persecution-related Bible access restrictions can make accessing Scripture difficult or dangerous, while socioeconomic barriers can put a Bible beyond people’s reach. Even where Scripture is available digitally, limited internet coverage or unsafe online environments can still prevent people from accessing it.”

Key barriers to access include persecution-related restrictions, social hostility toward Christians, threats from extremist groups, failing infrastructure, and socioeconomic issues, like poverty, lack of access to the internet, limited electricity, and illiteracy.

The top five countries on the coalition’s restrictions list (in order) are: Afghanistan, Yemen, Somalia, North Korea, and Eritrea.

“In Afghanistan, God’s Word is the most dangerous book any Afghan can possess,” the researchers stated. “And discovery can cost them their life. In North Korea, every dimension of Bible access is prohibited. Christians are treated as enemies of the state, and a Bible discovered in a routine house search can mean execution or a life sentence in a forced labor camp.”

The analysis looked at places, too, where believers don’t face legal restrictions but are suffering shortage of Bible access. Those top five countries (in order) are: the Democratic Republic of Congo (>10 million), Ethiopia (>10 million), Nigeria (>10 million), India (>10 million), and Uganda (5-10 million).

For context, there are more than 107 million Christians living in the DR Congo, but not even half — fewer than 33% — of believers there own a Bible in a country where it is legal to possess one.

“No law restricts access,” according to the report. “[But] the DRC is among the poorest countries in the world. Only about one in five people have electricity, and poor roads make remote communities difficult to reach in a country the size of Western Europe.”

items.title: Filmmaker Reveals What Charlie Kirk Said About Biblical Prophecy Before His Death
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "God's speaking to you."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Matthew Thayer’s new movie, “Can You Hear Me Now?” tackles biblical prophecy, exploring whether prophets still deliver messages to the masses today.

As part of the film, Thayer did one of the final interviews with conservative commentator Charlie Kirk before his assassination.

“I interviewed him with the impetus of talking to him about … the separation of church and state, Christian nationalism, all of the stuff that he was so eloquent at communicating,” Thayer said. “And it was a great interview.”

The filmmaker said he asked Kirk about prophecy and for his general take on whether it still occurs today.

“What he said blew me away,” said Thayer. “[Kirk’s] like, ‘Yeah, absolutely. I believe that there’s prophets, there’s prophecy — it’s a gift.’ It can be abused, but he’s seen it work and he’s seen it transform lives. But one of the things that he said that I thought was just right on was that a word from a prophet is not an excuse for … [inaction] or apathy.”

Kirk worried people might not have worked as hard as they could have in the 2020 election because they were relying on what they were told by a prophet and assumed it would be easily won.

“That actually, to me, points to a real fatalistic viewpoint that’s prevalent within the church of the will of God,” Thayer said. “That, if God speaks, it’s just going to happen. I don’t have to do anything about it. I can just pop some corn and sit on my couch and watch it all happen.”

Conversely, he said, a prophet’s role is to show up and alert people that situations are going the wrong way.

“A prophet’s word should be directional and actually require action upon the people and upon the people that are hearing it,” Thayer continued.

Ultimately, Thayer said he hopes “Can You Hear Me Now?” will inspire people to think deeper about how God might be speaking to them today.

“The biggest thing that was really kind of stuck with me the entire last year as we were making this film was all of the people that came out after Charlie Kirk’s death and were posting online going, ‘I’m being drawn to the Bible … Why do I want to go to church? I’m going to go to church’ — that was God speaking to all of those people.”

Thayer continued, “And so I really had a heart to really reach those people who are really infants in Christ and … kind of grab them by the collar and just go, ‘God’s speaking to you’ … because … there’s a whole swath of Christianity that doesn’t believe that God really kind of speaks.”

items.title: Is This News or Truth?
items.author: Lysa Terkeurst
items.summary: News and truth aren’t always one and the same. I learned this through a medical situation I faced a few years ago. It all started with words from my doctor that I never expected to hear. “Lysa, I’m so sorry. You have cancer.” I wish I could properly describe what happened in that moment. Everything&
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

News and truth aren’t always one and the same.

I learned this through a medical situation I faced a few years ago. It all started with words from my doctor that I never expected to hear.

“Lysa, I’m so sorry. You have cancer.”

I wish I could properly describe what happened in that moment. Everything around me got incredibly quiet and seemed to move very slowly. I could hear the doctor continuing to talk, but I couldn’t make out his words. I could feel words trying to form in my mouth, but there was no energy to actually speak. I knew I should probably cry, but no tears seemed available.

I am absolutely a woman who believes with all my heart that the presence of God is in the midst of my life. But in that moment, He felt distant and mysterious. I just felt stunned. And then I felt okay. And then I felt stunned again.

I wanted to hold it together. But then falling apart seemed quite reasonable.

It’s scary when doctors shock you with test results, and you don’t know what the future holds. I had come to the end of what I could do. I was forced to accept the harsh reality that there was nothing I could do to fix or change any of this.

In the days that followed my cancer news, God tenderly reminded me of an email my sweet friend Shaunti once sent me about another difficulty I was walking through. Her note said, “Lysa, this is news. This is not truth.”

Wow.

I’ve always thought of news and truth as one and the same. What the doctor gave me was news. Honest news, based on test results and medical facts.

But I have access to a truth that transcends news. The restoration that is impossible with human limitations is always possible for a limitless God. Truth is what factors God into the equation.

So, I found myself looking at the word impossible a little differently.

“Impossible,” in light of Shaunti’s note, could be completely different if I just stick an apostrophe between the first two letters. Then it becomes I’m-Possible. God is the Great I AM. Therefore, He was my possibility for hope and healing.

I’m-Possible is a much more comforting way to look at anything that feels quite impossible.

I suspect many of us have things in our life that feel impossible. Maybe you just got some bad news. News of an impossible financial situation. News of an impossible job situation. News of an impossible kid situation. News of an impossible friend situation. News of an impossible medical situation.

You may feel like you’re spiraling. You may feel like you want to try to take control to get to a different outcome. You may be wondering how God could let this happen. Trust me when I say I understand. Whatever news you just got or will get, I pray Shaunti’s advice helps you, too.

That is news.

And this is God’s Truth:

I AM THE WAY AND THE TRUTH AND THE LIFE.
“I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

I AM FOREVER FAITHFUL.
“He is the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them — he remains faithful forever” (Psalm 146:6, NIV).

I AM WITH YOU.
“So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand” (Isaiah 41:10, NIV).

I AM HOLDING YOU.
“Yet I am always with you; you hold me by my right hand” (Psalm 73:23, NIV).

I AM YOUR HIDING PLACE.
“You are my hiding place; you will protect me from trouble and surround me with songs of deliverance” (Psalm 32:7, NIV).

One of the greatest comforts to me through all I went through was knowing that somehow, God would use it for good. And that God would be my possible in the midst of what can sometimes feel so impossible.

Of course, I still have those less spiritually secure moments when I feel like I’m going to lose my mind. And cry. And doubt that God will bring about good from what feels impossibly hard. But He will. He didn’t answer my prayers exactly as I hoped with my diagnosis and yes, I had to go through a battle, but today I’m cancer free.

I don’t know what the future holds but what I do know is how thankful I am for the Great I AM. The One who will absolutely “Guide me in [His] truth and teach me” (Psalm 25:5a, NIV).

I love you, sweet friend. And I’m praying for you today. Praying that every time the word impossible creeps up and starts to steal your hope, you will see the words I’m-Possible and hold on to Him.

ABOUT LYSA TERKEURST: Lysa TerKeurst is president and chief visionary officer of Proverbs 31 Ministries and the author of seven New York Times bestsellers, including I Want to Trust You, But I Don’t, Good Boundaries and Goodbyes, Forgiving What You Can’t Forget, and It’s Not Supposed to Be This Way. Her latest book is Making Peace With What I Can’t Control. She enjoys life with her husband, Chaz, and her kids and grandkids. Connect with her at www.LysaTerKeurst.com or on social media @LysaTerKeurst.

items.title: St. Bartolo Longo Transformed Pompeii Through the Rosary
items.author: Margaret Peppiatt
items.summary:
Margaret Peppiatt

In 2025, Pope Leo XIV canonized a saint who transformed Pompeii through the Rosary, turning the once-ruined city into a life-giving source of God’s grace.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Margaret Peppiatt

Everyone knows the tragedy of Pompeii. Mt. Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, covering the ancient Roman city in volcanic ash and pumice. The name Pompeii accordingly conjures pictures of disaster, despair, and ultimately death in the public imagination. But the calamity is only part of the story—and certainly not the end of it. In 2025, Pope Leo XIV canonized a saint who transformed Pompeii through the Rosary, turning the once-ruined city into a life-giving source of God’s grace.

In 1872, an Italian lawyer named Bartolo Longo visited Pompeii on a business trip. About a decade earlier, the excavation of the historic site had come under the direction of the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli. However, Longo wasn’t interested in the excavations. He became more concerned with the living inhabitants of Pompeii, having found the local population dwelling in a rural area plagued by poverty—both physical and spiritual.

The superstitious beliefs and occult practices in Pompeii appalled Longo. He himself had been involved in a Satanic group before his conversion, so he was very familiar with the danger of these practices. According to accounts of his life, Longo had previously been initiated as a Satanic priest while studying at the University of Naples. Likely due to the prayers of his devout Catholic family back home, he eventually connected with a Dominican priest through a professor. Within a matter of a few weeks, Longo confessed his sins and left Satanism behind him.

Longo could therefore relate to the spiritual destitution he found in Pompeii on some level. He was probably even more shocked by the lack of educational and religious institutions in the area. Virtually no schools existed, which meant the local children did not get a basic education. Most of the farmers were illiterate. The small and dilapidated parish church had no sacristy or rectory; the pastor lived on a farm three miles away. As a result, people were not receiving any catechetical instruction. 

The field of Pompeii was evidently ready to be sown with the seeds of the Gospel. God chose Longo to be the sower. The Italian lawyer heard his calling through a profound spiritual experience that happened early on during his time in Pompeii. In a moment of utter despair over his past, Longo began questioning whether his commitment to Satanism was irrevocable and permanent. How could God save a man who had once pledged his life to the devil? Longo said he even felt tempted to commit suicide. Suddenly, he heard the voice of his confessor speaking the words of the Blessed Mother in his ear: “Whoever spreads the Rosary is saved.” This simple phrase cleared up the doubts tormenting him and fueled his commitment to propagating the Rosary.

After Longo’s conversion in Naples, a priest had told him that if he remained a layman, then God would call him to a specific apostolate. This was the apostolate: bringing the Christian faith to Pompeii through the Rosary. God had been preparing him for the task, as Longo had already become a Third Order Dominican. In 1874, Longo returned to Pompeii and began distributing Rosaries. He was accompanied and aided by the Countess Mariana di Fusco, the client on behalf of whom he had initially gone to Pompeii. They later entered into a Josephite marriage to avoid scandal while advancing their charitable work.

Order Your Set Today

For the rest of his life, the Rosary remained Longo’s primary means of evangelization. He proclaimed the Gospel to an uncatechized population through this Marian devotion. The Mysteries enabled people to easily grasp the key events of Christ’s life, making the Rosary the perfect tool for evangelization. In fact, Pope St. John Paul II later referred to the Rosary as the “the compendium of the Gospel.” Longo repeatedly stressed the importance of meditating on the Mysteries, particularly through his publication Fifteen Saturdays in 1877. He helped the Fifteen Saturdays devotion spread worldwide, and it received support from Pope Leo XIII, the “Pope of the Rosary.”

In a matter of just a few decades, Pompeii was transformed into a place of life. The Sanctuary of Pompeii was consecrated in 1891, eventually becoming an international pilgrimage site that still welcomes over two million visitors annually. During his 2026 pastoral visit to Pompeii, Pope Leo XIV recalled Longo’s legacy, noting that he was not only an apostle of the Rosary but also of charity. Prayer laid the foundation for his work, ensuring that his efforts at reviving the region were fruitful. Longo took a holistic approach to reviving Pompeii, overseeing economic and social developments that occurred in tandem with the area’s spiritual rebirth. He started schools and orphanages, showing particular care for the children of convicted criminals.

In Fifteen Saturdays, Longo referred to the incredible story of Pompeii as the “greatest miracle in modern times.” He always saw himself as a humble instrument reliant on the intercession of the Blessed Mother. “The work of Pompeii is the work of God! The Virgin Mary is directing it to His glory, and the means of promulgation, of which she avails herself, are miracles!” Longo saw the merciful love of God as the moving force behind the transformation of Pompeii. He believed that Mary chose the city to be a sign of God’s mercy for the entire world. 

The story of Pompeii serves as inspiration in a world that has largely embraced a culture of death. A kind of resurrection occurred in Pompeii through Mary’s intercession, infusing life into a place historically tied to paganism and death. During his homily at the sanctuary on May 8 this year, Pope Leo XIV reiterated a statement that Pope John Paul II made there over two decades ago: “Today, as in the times of ancient Pompeii, it is vital to proclaim Christ to a society that is drifting away from Christian values and even forgetting about them.” In order to bring about a culture of life, the faithful must undertake evangelization in a spirit of prayer, just as Longo depended upon the Rosary to nourish his own interior life and share the Gospel with others.

items.title: Monday, October 5, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus affirms a scholar’s identification of the greatest commandment:
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 1:6-12

I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting the one who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another gospel, but there are some who are confusing you and want to pervert the gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should proclaim to you a gospel contrary to what we proclaimed to you, let that one be accursed! As we have said before, so now I repeat, if anyone proclaims to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let that one be accursed!

Am I now seeking human approval, or God’s approval? Or am I trying to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ.

For I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that the gospel that was proclaimed by me is not of human origin; for I did not receive it from a human source, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

Psalm
Psalm 111:1b-2, 7-8, 9, 10c

Praise the Lord!
I will give thanks to the Lord with my whole heart,
    in the company of the upright, in the congregation.
Great are the works of the Lord,
    studied by all who delight in them.
Praise the Lord!
I will give thanks to the Lord with my whole heart,
    in the company of the upright, in the congregation.
Great are the works of the Lord,
    studied by all who delight in them.
He sent redemption to his people;
    he has commanded his covenant forever.
    Holy and awesome is his name.
The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom;
    all those who practice it have a good understanding.
    His praise endures forever.

Gospel Reading
Luke 10:25-37

Just then a lawyer stood up to test Jesus. “Teacher,” he said, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” He said to him, “What is written in the law? What do you read there?” He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.” And he said to him, “You have given the right answer; do this, and you will live.”

But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell into the hands of robbers, who stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road; and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. But a Samaritan while traveling came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with pity. He went to him and bandaged his wounds, having poured oil and wine on them. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. The next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said, ‘Take care of him; and when I come back, I will repay you whatever more you spend.’ Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?” He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus affirms a scholar’s identification of the greatest commandment: “You shall love the Lord, your God, with all your heart, with all your being, with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.”

All of religion is finally about awakening the deepest desire of the heart and directing it toward God; it is about the ordering of love toward that which is most worthy of love. But, Jesus says, a necessary implication of this love of God is compassion for one’s fellow human beings.

Why are the two commandments so tightly linked? The best response is the simplest: because of who Jesus is. Christ is not simply a human being, and he is not simply God; rather, he is the God-man, the one in whose person divinity and humanity meet.

Therefore, it is finally impossible to love him as God without loving the humanity that he has, in his own person, embraced. Those who know Christ Jesus, fully divine and fully human, realize that the love of God necessarily draws us to a love for the human race. They grasp the logical consistency and spiritual integrity of the greatest commandment.
